case_studies.title: Better Harnesses, Smaller Models: Building 90% Cheaper Agents via Automated Harness Adaptation
case_studies.abstract: Frontier LLM agents are automating many business tasks, but their high inference cost makes large-scale deployment unsustainable. Small language models (SLMs) offer a cheaper alternative, yet they typically fall short when swapped into a harness designed for a frontier LLM. We show that for many routine business tasks, SLM agents can match LLM performance at 90% lower cost, when paired with an adapted harness that can be automatically discovered by a meta agent. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of high costs associated with using large language models for business tasks by building smaller models with adapted harnesses, resulting in 90% lower costs. The team built a meta agent that can automatically discover and adapt harnesses for smaller language models, allowing them to match the performance of larger models. This could impact cloud infrastructure costs for businesses using language models.

case_studies.abstract: Modern LLMs are increasingly deployed in long-context applications such as retrieval-augmented generation, repository-level coding, and agentic workflows whose accumulated reasoning and tool traces routinely push the input an order of magnitude past the pretraining window, making zero-shot context extension the dominant deployment path for open-weight checkpoints. case_studies.summary: Researchers built Jet-Long, a new method to improve long-context applications for large language models, solving the problem of limited context window sizes. Jet-Long achieves efficient long-context extension with dynamic bifocal RoPE, resulting in better performance for applications like retrieval-augmented generation and repository-level coding. case_studies.title: SigLIP-HD by Fine-to-Coarse Supervision
case_studies.abstract: High-quality visual representation is a long-standing pursuit in computer vision. In the context of multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), feeding higher-resolution images can produce more fine-grained visual tokens. However, it introduces additional computational and design complexity, due to multiple forward passes and post-processing of increased tokens. Before simply adopting a higher resolution, have we truly unlocked the model's full perception capability at a standard resolution? Therefore, we study an interesting problem: how to achieve fine visual perception under lower cost without larger images.
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of achieving fine visual perception in computer vision without using higher-resolution images, by building a model called SigLIP-HD that uses fine-to-coarse supervision, resulting in improved visual representation at a lower computational cost. The model enables multimodal large language models to produce more detailed visual tokens without increasing image resolution. This is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

In this work, the mutable component of that context is a persistent system-level instruction that is updated from operational experience while the model, tools, and harness remain fixed. case_studies.title: Self-Guided Test-Time Training for Long-Context LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Long-context processing has become increasingly important for large language models (LLMs), but simply extending the context window does not guarantee effective utilization of long inputs. As input length grows, accuracy often degrades, indicating that models still struggle to identify and use the evidence most relevant to a question. A promising way to improve long-context utilization is test-time training (TTT), which treats the test context as a training example for instance-specific parameter adaptation. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of long-context processing in large language models by building a self-guided test-time training method, which resulted in improved accuracy without requiring extensive computational resources. The method allows models to adapt to specific input instances at test time, enhancing their ability to identify relevant information. This research is not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: ProofCouncil: An LLM Agent for Solving Open Mathematical Problems
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in solving open problems in mathematics. However, their performance can be further improved through agentic workflows tailored to real-world mathematical practice. To this end, we introduce ProofCouncil, a mathematical agent that is designed to tackle open problems using an author-critic architecture. ProofCouncil served as a submission to the second batch of FirstProof, a challenge consisting of 10 real-world mathematical problems that agents must solve autonomously. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of using large language models to tackle open mathematical problems by building an agent called ProofCouncil, which achieved promising results in a mathematical challenge. The agent was able to autonomously solve 6 out of 10 real-world mathematical problems. This research is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.

case_studies.title: Failure as a Process: An Anatomy of CLI Coding Agent Trajectories
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents are increasingly deployed to autonomously perform software engineering tasks in terminal-based environments, making their reliability a growing concern. Existing empirical studies investigate why coding agents fail, yet they largely treat failure as a final outcome rather than a temporal process, providing limited insight into how failures emerge, evolve, and become unrecoverable. case_studies.summary: This research investigates the reliability of large language model coding agents used in terminal-based environments, specifically how failures emerge and evolve over time. The authors built a process-oriented framework to analyze failure trajectories. The result provides insight into the temporal process of coding agent failures, which can help improve their reliability.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that uses large language model coding agents, here is what to do: review your agents' failure logs to identify patterns of failure onset and evolution, assess your agents' recovery mechanisms, and consider implementing additional reliability measures based on the research findings.

case_studies.title: Conceptual Networks for Cross-Linguistic Idiomatic Expressions:A Feature-Based Graph Approach
case_studies.abstract: We present an interpretable network-based framework for representing idiomatic and figurative meaning across eight typologically diverse languages, totaling 160 conventional expressions, the large majority of which are idiomatic. Each expression is annotated with binary conceptual features (containment, concealment, emotional, social, etc.) derived from cognitive-linguistic theory, and pairwise Jaccard similarities define a weighted graph. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of understanding idiomatic expressions across different languages by building a network-based framework that represents their meanings. The result is a weighted graph that clusters idioms by conceptual schema rather than language. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: VEXAIoT: Autonomous IoT Vulnerability EXploitation using AI Agents
case_studies.abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) systems are inherently vulnerable due to constrained hardware, outdated firmware, and insecure default configurations, creating a need for scalable and adaptive security testing approaches. While recent adoptions of Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated promise in penetration testing and Capture-the-Flag (CTF) environments, their application to IoT specific vulnerabilities remains unexplored. This paper presents an autonomous multi-agent framework, referred to as Vulnerability EXploitation using AI Agents (VEXAIoT), for vulnerability discovery and exploit
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of insecure Internet of Things (IoT) systems by building an autonomous framework called VEXAIoT, which uses AI agents to discover and exploit vulnerabilities, resulting in a more scalable and adaptive security testing approach. The framework was tested and demonstrated promise in identifying IoT-specific vulnerabilities. This research aims to improve the security of IoT systems.

case_studies.abstract: Enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents requires effective orchestration of diverse expert models and tools. However, existing frameworks typically call APIs based on coarse-grained matching between tasks and the functions of expert models or tools, while overlooking critical factors such as performance variability and cost efficiency among functionally similar alternatives. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inefficient task allocation in large language model agents by introducing an auction-based framework called Agora. The researchers built a framework that dynamically allocates tasks to expert models and tools based on performance and cost efficiency. The result is improved reasoning capabilities in LLM agents.

The effectiveness of this process hinges on the quality of review comments. As large language models (LLMs) gain traction in automating code review tasks, the utility of these systems is directly limited by the quality of the datasets on which they are trained. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of poor quality code review comments by building an LLM-based curation pipeline to improve the quality of these comments, resulting in more accurate and helpful feedback for developers. The pipeline helps to balance the usefulness and naturalness of code review comments. This research aims to improve the datasets used to train large language models for code review tasks.
